The next PR should be:

**`fix(checkout): isolate seat holds per checkout`**, referencing [roadmap issue #74](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/74).

### Roadmap status

PR [#91](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/pull/91) moved the roadmap from `REAL_WORLD_ROADMAP.md` into GitHub issues and phase milestones. The repository now explicitly treats those issues as the source of truth ([AGENTS.md](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/AGENTS.md:703)).

| Roadmap area | Current state |
|---|---|
| Phase 0, #63–#67 | Complete |
| Phase 1, #68–#72 | Complete |
| P2.1, #73 | Complete |
| P2.2, #74 | Partially complete |
| P2.3, #75 | Waiting behind #74 |
| P2.4, #76 | Five main slices merged; rebooking split to #234 |
| P2.5, #77 | Not started |
| Phases 3–5 | Later work |

There are currently **no open PRs**, and local `main` is clean and synchronized at [`55f25db`](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/commit/55f25db413683aa2faa8e0ea53b0639a4117f712).

### Why this PR is next

PR [#257](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/pull/257) delivered the first #74 slice: expiring holds and automatic abandonment/release behavior. Its follow-up comment records a verified defect: `holderKey` is currently the user ID, so two checkout tabs belonging to the same user can release or refresh each other’s seats.

The current code confirms that:

- Hold claims and releases use `session.user.id` ([actions.ts](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/app/actions.ts:423)).
- `SeatClaim` anticipates a future checkout-scoped identity but does not have one yet ([seatHolds.ts](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/lib/seatHolds.ts:23)).
- The wizard does not create its request identifier until booking submission, after seats were held ([BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx](/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/travel-app/components/ui/BookingCheckoutWizard.tsx:696)).

The PR should:

- Establish a validated checkout identifier before the first hold.
- Scope claim, refresh, visibility, and release operations to that checkout.
- Ensure two tabs for one account cannot interfere with each other.
- Add database concurrency, component, and browser coverage.
- Leave atomic hold-to-booking conversion and the visible expiry/recovery countdown for subsequent #74 slices.

That is the smallest independently shippable slice and removes a prerequisite blocker before the more delicate transaction work.

content.text: why is each jest project run seperately? I would think it would run the unit tess, then the end to end tests

There are two Jest projects here, then a separate end-to-end suite:

1. `test:unit` — fast unit/component tests, no shared database.
2. `test:database` — Jest tests against shared Postgres, forced serially.
3. `npx playwright test` — the actual browser end-to-end tests.

The repository’s `npm test` is just `test:unit && test:database`. Because the unit project has two known pre-existing failures, that command would stop immediately and never run the database project. Running the two Jest projects separately ensures both are genuinely checked and reported, then Playwright runs afterward for E2E. It also prevents database tests from being accidentally parallelized against the same tables.

- five focused mutants killed and independently audited

  draft: false,
  maintainer_can_modify: true,
  body: `## Summary

- scope each hold to one authenticated user's checkout UUID instead of the user alone
- reuse the booking idempotency UUID from seat review through booking cleanup
- keep generic occupied-seat reads conservative when no checkout identity is available
- cover same-account tabs through component, PostgreSQL, and browser journeys
- make conflict copy truthful when the competing checkout belongs to the same account

Part of #74.

## Why

PR #257 introduced expiring holds, but used the user id as the holder key. Two tabs for the same signed-in customer therefore stomped each other: changing seats in one checkout released the other checkout's claims. Binding the existing booking request UUID to the authenticated user isolates those tabs without letting the browser choose a complete holder key.

## User impact

Two checkout tabs on the same account can hold different seats independently. Completing one booking releases only that checkout's holds; the other tab remains actionable.

## Remaining #74 work

- convert holds atomically when booking completes
- display hold expiry and recovery behavior

Concurrent-checkout hold limits are tracked separately in #269. The unrelated Travel Guide Playwright 404 flake observed during verification is tracked in #268.

The thin slice is now defined: booking must consume only this checkout’s live holds in the same transaction that writes seat assignments; another checkout’s hold must block it; expired/missing holds must not be silently treated as ownership; retries must stay idempotent; and every transaction touching multiple flights/seats must lock in one deterministic order. I’ve finished tracing the current boundaries. The key is to make holding and booking share the same ordered flight lock; otherwise “check then delete” still leaves an insert race. I’m prototyping that lock discipline against PostgreSQL now before changing the branch.

+## Summary
+
+- serialize multi-flight and multi-seat hold mutations behind stable `Flight` locks

content.text:
The next PR should be [#269 — Cap concurrent seat-hold checkouts per account](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/269).

Why it should precede #75:

- It closes the inventory-abuse gap discovered during #74.
- It is a bounded hardening slice while the hold design is fresh.
- Payments would otherwise build on an inventory system one account can temporarily exhaust with unlimited checkout UUIDs.
- There are no open PRs, and `main` is clean.

Recommended policy: permit two concurrent checkout IDs per account, preserving the tested two-tab journey. Enforce it transactionally with a per-user database lock, return a recoverable error for a third checkout, and cover simultaneous requests with PostgreSQL tests.

After that, the next main roadmap feature is [#75 — Integrate real payments safely](https://github.com/scottdensmore/travel-app/issues/75). That should begin with a plan/prototype for Stripe sandbox authorization-before-booking.

Housekeeping: #256’s seat-map overflow appears resolved by PR #273; #193 remains open for its separate clipped mobile-navigation problem.

const body="## Summary

- cap one authenticated account at two concurrent live seat-hold checkouts
- serialize account admission before flight inventory locks so simultaneous checkouts on different flights cannot bypass the cap
- keep existing checkouts refreshable, ignore expired and other-account holds, and return a focused recoverable alert for a refused third checkout

Ok lets pick up 75.

I’m picking up #75 as the next Phase 2 item. I’ll first map the current booking/payment boundary and settle the smallest shippable slice; because payment ordering is security- and data-sensitive, I’ll use a short prototype before committing to schema or provider integration, then follow the repository’s branch-first TDD workflow for implementation.

Baseline on clean `main` is recorded: lint has 0 errors and the same 8 warnings; unit is 735/735. The current app has no payment SDK or card collection—only a nullable `paymentIntentId`, confirmed-by-default bookings, and cancellation amounts prepared for future refunds—so the first slice must change the booking authority, not merely add a checkout widget.

The key design constraint is now clear: Stripe and PostgreSQL cannot share a transaction. Capturing before the booking risks charging without a seat; confirming a booking before capture risks issuing an unpaid ticket. I’m prototyping the safer saga boundary against current Stripe guidance: authorize first, create a non-confirmed booking while atomically consuming holds, capture, then let an idempotent signed webhook make it `CONFIRMED`.

- add PaymentAttempt schema constraints, a hand-authored migration, user-deletion retention, and Playwright leak tracking
- document the runtime-only Stripe secret and local test-mode setup

content.text: The prototype will enforce one important boundary: Stripe’s client result only signals “confirmation finished”; it never authorizes booking by itself. The app must re-read the PaymentIntent through the authenticated server action, and only `AUTHORIZED`/`CAPTURED` may reach booking creation. This keeps card fields inside Stripe’s iframe and keeps the server authoritative.

content.text: A design check caught an important edge before it escaped into implementation: one refund row cannot safely support a terminal Stripe failure and a later retry. Reusing the same idempotency key would keep returning the failed refund, while replacing its provider ID would erase audit history. I’m correcting the prototype to model one durable refund request with append-only provider attempts; each retry gets its own durable idempotency key, and transport retries reuse the same attempt.

+-- Record when a payment first becomes captured so receipts do not mislabel

+-- Existing captured attempts use their last durable update as the best
+-- available historical value; new captures are stamped by the trigger.
+--
+-- To reverse:
+--
+--     BEGIN;
+--     DROP TRIGGER "PaymentAttempt_set_captured_at" ON "PaymentAttempt";
+--     DROP FUNCTION set_payment_attempt_captured_at();
+--     ALTER TABLE "PaymentAttempt"
+--       DROP CONSTRAINT "PaymentAttempt_captured_has_time",

+
+ALTER TABLE "PaymentAttempt"
+    ADD COLUMN "capturedAt" TIMESTAMP(3);
+
+UPDATE "PaymentAttempt"
+SET "capturedAt" = "updatedAt"
+WHERE "status" = 'CAPTURED';
+
+CREATE FUNCTION set_payment_attempt_captured_at()
+RETURNS trigger
+LANGUAGE plpgsql
+AS $$
+BEGIN
+    IF TG_OP = 'UPDATE' AND OLD."capturedAt" IS NOT NULL THEN
+        NEW."capturedAt" := OLD."capturedAt";
+    ELSIF NEW."status" = 'CAPTURED' AND NEW."capturedAt" IS NULL THEN
+        NEW."capturedAt" := CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;
